excerpts.text: The **mole** (symbol **mol**) is a [unit of measurement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unit_of_measurement "Unit of measurement"), the [base unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit") in the [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units "International System of Units") (SI) for *[amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance")*.
The mole was made the seventh [SI base unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit") in 1971 by the 14th CGPM.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Before the [2019 revision of the SI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_revision_of_the_SI "2019 revision of the SI"), the mole was defined as the amount of substance of a system that contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 12 [grams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gram "Gram") of [carbon-12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon-12 "Carbon-12") (the most common [isotope of carbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotopes_of_carbon "Isotopes of carbon")).[[21]](#cite_note-SI8-21) The term *gram-molecule* was formerly used to mean one mole of molecules, and *gram-atom* for one mole of atoms.[[17]](#cite_note-SI114-15-17) For example, 1 mole of [MgBr2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MgBr2 "MgBr2") is 1 gram-molecule of MgBr2 but 3 gram-atoms of MgBr2.[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[23]](#cite_note-23)

excerpts.text: In 2019, four of the seven [SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit") specified in the [International System of Quantities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Quantities "International System of Quantities") were redefined in terms of natural physical constants, rather than human artefacts such as the [International Prototype of the Kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Prototype_of_the_Kilogram "International Prototype of the Kilogram").[[1]](#cite_note-SI-statement-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Effective 20 May 2019, the 144th anniversary of the [Metre Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metre_Convention "Metre Convention"), the [kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram"), [ampere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampere "Ampere"), [kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin"), and [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)") are defined by setting exact numerical values, when expressed in SI units, for the [Planck constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planck_constant "Planck constant") (*h*), the [elementary electric charge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elementary_electric_charge "Elementary electric charge") (*e*), the [Boltzmann constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boltzmann_constant "Boltzmann constant") (*k*B), and the [Avogadro constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avogadro_constant "Avogadro constant") (*N*A), respectively.

The revised definition breaks that link by making a mole a specific number of entities of the substance in question.

* **Previous definition**: The mole is the [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance") of a system that contains as many elementary entities as there are [atoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atom "Atom") in 0.012 kilogram of [carbon-12](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon-12 "Carbon-12"). When the mole is used, the elementary entities must be specified and may be atoms, [molecules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecule "Molecule"), [ions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ion "Ion"), [electrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electron "Electron"), other particles, or specified groups of such particles.
* **2019 definition**:[[7]](#cite_note-cipm_106-7): 22 The mole, symbol mol, is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076×1023 elementary entities. This number is the fixed numerical value of the [Avogadro constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avogadro_constant "Avogadro constant"), *N*A, when expressed in the unit mol−1 and is called the Avogadro number.[[7]](#cite_note-cipm_106-7)[[48]](#cite_note-55) The amount of substance, symbol *n*, of a system is a measure of the number of specified elementary entities. An elementary entity may be an atom, a molecule, an ion, an electron, any other particle or specified group of particles.
